The watch trade moved its tariff fight from the invoice to the courtroom. Collective Horology, a California retailer, sued at the US Court of International Trade — arguing Washington slapped a near-uniform tariff on dozens of countries without the country-by-country analysis the 1974 Trade Act requires.

The stakes are concrete: Swiss watches have run at least 12.5% more expensive since April 2025, and Collective says it's still owed $164,000 in refunds from tariffs the Supreme Court already vacated. It's the first watch retailer to fight the regime rather than just pay it.

The trade's price book just admitted something. GemGuide — the pricing service the American colored-stone trade leans on — raised Mozambique ruby prices sharply on demand for unenhanced material, then rebuilt its Burma section from scratch.

The striking part: it abandoned the traditional one-to-ten quality scale for untreated Burmese ruby and now publishes only four grades — Middle Commercial, Lower Good, Upper Fine and Upper Extra Fine. Research director Stuart Robertson says Mozambique prices have, in effect, skyrocketed as tender buyers chase clean goods. The Burma change is the quieter admission: fine Mogok material reaches the market so rarely that availability now matters more than price.

The revisions are live in the app now and reach print in the July–August issue — which means the number under a ruby changed this week whether or not the stone did.

India's largest branded jeweller keeps printing the same remarkable number. Titan's June quarter revenue rose about 41% — its third straight quarter above 40% — led by a jewellery arm (Tanishq, Mia, CaratLane) up 39%.

The texture is the whole trade's story in one line: buyer growth in the early double digits, but average ticket sizes up in the high double digits. More customers, each spending markedly more, against stable gold. Watches grew 23%, eyewear 23%, and the small international business 128%.
